result: eLife is implementing new policies to curtail requests for additional experiments during revisions in response to COVID-19. Manuscripts that meet eLife standards will be accepted without delay even if additional data would strengthen them (C6, C7), with revisions limited to clarity and presentation. Papers requiring modest additional data will be accepted with modified claims and expectations for future follow-up work (C8, C9).
evaluation: The policy changes are clearly articulated as institutional decisions (C6-C12) with explicit rationale tied to COVID-19 impacts (C5). The claims describe existing policy context (C1-C4) and the specific modifications being implemented. These are policy announcements rather than empirical findings, so they are supported by institutional authority and stated intent.

result: eLife is suspending its typical two-month limit for manuscript revisions, allowing authors unlimited time to submit revised manuscripts until the research enterprise fully restarts. This applies to papers currently in revision and any submissions made during the pandemic.
evaluation: This policy change is explicitly stated (C15) with clear scope definition (C16) and context about the existing policy (C14). As an institutional policy announcement, it is supported by the authority of the journal's editorial leadership.

result: eLife is making preprint posting to bioRxiv or medRxiv the default for all submissions, while allowing authors to opt out. The journal cites the success of preprints during COVID-19 research (C17-C19) as motivation and is developing systems to attach peer reviews to preprints on bioRxiv (C27, C28).
evaluation: The policy change itself is clearly stated (C23, C24), but the supporting claims about preprints speeding COVID-19 research (C18) and facilitating public understanding (C19) are presented as observations without empirical evidence or citations. These are plausible assertions but lack quantitative support or systematic analysis to verify the claimed benefits.

result: eLife is clarifying and extending its 'scoop protection' policy to explicitly cover preprints in addition to peer-reviewed articles. Work done simultaneously by multiple groups will not be considered less significant due to another group's preprint posting (C32), and this does not change the journal's approach to replication studies (C33-C35).
evaluation: This represents a clarification and extension of existing policy (C29, C31) with specific operational details (C32). The policy is clearly articulated with appropriate context about what is and is not changing (C33-C35). As a policy statement, it is supported by institutional authority.

result: eLife is accelerating its plan to invite early-career researchers to serve as reviewing editors, building on a successful trial of using them as reviewers. This aims to provide editorial experience opportunities and diversify the editorial board.
evaluation: While the policy change is clearly stated (C39-C41) and builds on described prior work (C36-C38), the claim that the earlier trial was 'successful' (C37) lacks supporting metrics or evidence. The success claim is asserted but not demonstrated with data on outcomes, quality of reviews, or other measurable indicators.

result: eLife acknowledges that its editors, reviewers, and staff may not be able to operate at peak efficiency during the pandemic due to competing demands on their time.
evaluation: This is a straightforward acknowledgment of operational constraints during the pandemic (C43, C44). As a statement of institutional expectations and circumstances, it requires no empirical validation and is supported by the general context of pandemic disruptions.
